## Ion Torrent

`One molecule, one bead, one bubble, one well`

* emPCR for clonal amplification
    * DNA fragments or amplicons, adapters are ligated to both ends
        * More beads than DNA molecules
        * Adapters serves as PCR priming sites
        * ... 'primers' are attached to the beads
    * Beads are embedded in oil droplets
        * one bead per droplet
        * Micro PCR vesecle
    * Vesecles are disrupted

---

* Wells fit only one bead
* Amplification with only one of A,C,G,T provided at a time
* Incorporation of a dNTP yields a proton / $H^+$ ion
* pH changes releative to the number of specific dNTP incorporation

::: {#fig-clonal layout-ncol=1}

![](media/IonTor_pic.png){width=50%}

Escalante AE, et al (2014) DOI: 10.7550/rmb.43498.

:::


## Ion Torrnet: Pros vs Cons

* Pros: Faster, cheeper, natural chemistry, no ropes and pulleys 
* Cons: Homopolymer issues, `slightly` lower Q-scores compared to Illumina

## Stems from older Roche 454 sequencing

* $PP_i$ + adenosine $5′$ phosphosulfate + **ATP sulfurylase** $->$ ATP + $SO_4^{-2}$
* ATP + luciferin + **luciferase** $->$ AMP + $PP_i$ + oxyluciferin + $CO_2$ ​+ light
* The enzyme apyrase degrades ATP and any unused or unincorporated nucleotides

::: {#fig-roche454 layout-ncol=1}

![](media/firefly.gif){width=70%}

Flux AI: Depict fireflies in photorealistic style

:::


## Illumina sequencing

`clonal 'pixels' by bridge amplification`

::: {#fig-roche454 layout-ncol=1}

![](media/flux_bamboo_forest.png){width=80%}

Flux AI: Depict a bamboo forest in photo realistic style

:::

## Principle

* Library prep
    * DNA is fragmented, typically transposons/transposases are used, but other fragmentation methods also exist
*   Clonal amplification
    * Bridge amplification is used rather than emulsion PCR (emPCR)
    * This happens on flow cell clusters and not beads

--- 

* In each cycle all four nucleotides are available
    * They are fluorescently labeled AND 3` terminus is blocked
    * The incorporated nucleotide is excited by light
    * The incorporated base is determined by the frequency of the light which was emitted
    * The 3` end is unblocked and a new cycle begins
        * Only one nucleotide can be incorporated in a cycle
        * The read length is determined by the number of cycles
* The DNA fragments are typically sequenced from both ends, resulting in paired reads



## Illumina: Sales pitch

* Pros: Does not suffer from homopolymer issues, higher Q-scores
* Cons: Slower, more expensive (modified dNTPS)

## ... Pros and cons

* Does not require clonal amplification
* Library preparation is much simpler
* Generates much longer reads
* Suffers from accuracy - or maybe not so much

If I have a 1 in 10 chance of an error, which is random:

$$(\frac{1}{10})^{10} = \frac{1}{10^{10}}$$


## PacBio Single-molecule real-time (SMRT)

* Library preparation
    * Formation of a SMRTbell as template
        * Closed single stranded circular DNA
        * This is achieved by ligating hairpin adaptors to both ends of the target dsDNA

::: {#fig-dumbell layout-ncol=1}

![](media/SMRTbell.png){width=100%}

Rhoads A and Fai Au K (2015), doi: 10.1016/j.gpb.2015.08.002

:::

---

* The SMRTbell is loaded onto chip and diffuses into one of many sequencing units, called a zero-mode waveguide ZMW
    * The smallest available volume for light detection, removing background
* Each one of these ZMWs have a DNA polymerase immobilized at the bottom
    * This polymerase can then bind to either of the hairpins
    * Fluorescent labeled nucleotides are provided to the ZMW and thus enzyme
        * Each of the 4 nucleotides are labeled with fluorophores emitting different wavelengths
            * Allows differentiation
        * Flourophores are covalently attached on the γ-phosphate
* On each incorporation of a labeled dNTP, a light pulse is produced

---

* Along with the the ZMW a camera can record these light flashes and the sequenced is deduced
* A single pass results in a sequence accuracy of 11-15%
    * However, since the template is circular, multiple passes is possible
        * Due to the randomness of error an accuracy rate of ~99.9% is possible
        * Sequencing and passes are possible until the enzyme stops working or for the duration of the enzymes lifetime
        * There is a tradeof between sequence accuracy and read length

::: {#fig-pacbio-qual layout-ncol=1}

![](media/pacbio_reads.png){width=30%}

https://www.pacb.com/technology/hifi-sequencing/how-it-works/

:::

## The ONT principle

* Biological pores or transporters are embedded in a semiconductor chip
    * As particles pass through this chip the resistance over the membrane changes
* dsDNA or RNA is mixed with a motor protein which binds these molecules to the pores
* The DNA or RNA is threaded through the pores and the changes in current is recorded
* This wave pattern is used to infer the sequence
* Very long read lengths
* Can detect epigenetics
* They promise protein sequencing
    * Multi-omics

## Phred / Q-scores

Developed by Phil Green and Brent Ewing, 1990s

$$
Q=−10.log_{10}(p)
$${#eq-Q-score}

or

```
Q10 = 90%         (1/10 chance of an incorrect base call)
Q20 = 99%         (1/100 chance of an incorrect base call)
Q30 = 99.9%       (1/1,000 chance of an incorrect base call)
Q40 = 99.99%      (1/10,000 chance of an incorrect base call)
Q50 = 99.999%     (1/100,000 chance of an incorrect base call)
Q60 = 99.9999%    (1/1,000,000 chance of an incorrect base call)
```
    These have been adopted by NGS technologies and is encoded in the FASTQ files
